overview.title: Figure 16.6: splicing hard and soft tokens; the test image
overview.main_topic: Displaying the test image and the diagram of how image soft tokens and text hard tokens are merged before the Transformer
overview.central_idea: Figure 16.6 shows the mechanism from p.522. Text tokens (including `` placeholders) pass through the text-embedding matrix and become green 'hard' tokens. Image patches pass through the image encoder and become orange 'soft' tokens. The two are interleaved into one sequence for a stack of decoder blocks. Figure 16.7 is the test image used next.
overview.importance: The figure is the visual summary of how a decoder-only LLM such as Gemma becomes multimodal without changing its decoder blocks. The image shown is the input for the questions asked on p.524.
learning_objectives: Read figure 16.6: identify the text embedding, the image encoder, hard tokens, soft tokens, and the merged sequence.
Explain why the `` placeholder positions in the text are where the soft tokens end up.
Load an image file into a NumPy array with `keras.utils.load_img` and display it with matplotlib.
prerequisites: Hard vs. soft tokens and the (256, 2560) image representation (p.522)
The image download code on p.522

summary: This page is mostly visual and finishes the image-loading code from p.522. **Code.** The downloaded file at `image_path` is read with `keras.utils.load_img`, which returns a PIL image, and converted to a NumPy array with `np.array`, giving a `(height, width, 3)` uint8 array. It is then shown with matplotlib, with the axes hidden. The array `image` is what is passed to Gemma on p.524 (`"images": [image]`). **Figure 16.6, "Handling image input by splicing text tokens and soft image tokens together."** On the left, the text prompt `What is ?` passes through a grid labelled **Text embedding** (the embedding matrix). Each token becomes a green **"hard" token**. On the right, the image, drawn as four patches of the library scene, passes through a trapezoid labelled **Image encoder**, which emits orange **"soft" tokens**. At the bottom the two streams are merged into one sequence. Green tokens come first and last, and the orange soft tokens sit where the `` placeholders were. The merged sequence enters a box labelled **Transformer** that contains a stack of **Decoder block**s. The figure is schematic: it shows four placeholders and four patches, while the real Gemma model uses 256 (p.522). **Figure 16.7, "A test image for the Gemma model."** The image (the file is named `learned-python.png`) shows a snake wearing glasses, curled in a leather armchair in front of bookshelves, with an open book. The name is a pun: a learned "python". On p.524 Gemma is asked to describe it and to say what the snake is wearing.

concepts.name: Soft token (vs. hard token)
concepts.definition: A vector inserted directly into the Transformer's input sequence by another network (here the image encoder), rather than looked up by token ID in the embedding matrix.
concepts.intuition: In figure 16.6, green squares come from the dictionary (embedding grid); orange squares are custom-made by the image encoder.
concepts.technical: Hard: $E[t] \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$; soft: $f_{\text{enc}}(\text{patch}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, with the same $d$ (2560 for Gemma 3 4B).
concepts.example: Four `` placeholder positions in the figure are filled by four orange soft tokens.
concepts.misconception: That the `` placeholders' own embeddings are used. Their positions are overwritten by the encoder outputs (p.524).

concepts.name: Multimodal LLM
concepts.definition: A language model whose single input sequence mixes text embeddings and encoded non-text data.
concepts.intuition: Two on-ramps (text embedding, image encoder) feed one highway (the decoder stack).
concepts.technical: Merged sequence $X \in \mathbb{R}^{(n_{text}+n_{img}) \times d}$ processed by unchanged decoder blocks.
concepts.significance: Figure 16.6 shows that only the input side changes.
concepts.misconception: That the image goes through the text embedding grid; it bypasses it entirely.

deeper.title: Reading figure 16.6 step by step
deeper.body: 1. **Text in:** the prompt is tokenized into `What`, `is`, four `` placeholders, and `?`. 2. **Hard tokens:** each ID selects a row of the *Text embedding* grid, producing the seven green squares. 3. **Image in:** the picture is cut into patches (four in the drawing, 256 in Gemma). 4. **Soft tokens:** the *Image encoder* maps the patches to orange vectors of the same size as the green ones. 5. **Splice:** in the bottom row, the green tokens for `What` and `is` come first, then the orange tokens in the `` slots, then the green `?`. (The drawing shows two greens, four oranges, and one green.) 6. **Transformer:** the merged sequence goes through the stack of decoder blocks, which treat every position the same way.

deeper.title: What 'soft' buys you, visually
deeper.body: Beyond the book: one alternative is to *quantize* images into discrete codes (a learned 'visual vocabulary') and treat them as hard tokens. Some image-generation models do this. The soft-token design in figure 16.6 avoids that bottleneck because each orange vector is continuous. The trade-off is that the model cannot easily *output* soft tokens, which matches the remark on p.524 that the Transformer is not trained to output image soft tokens.

misconceptions.correction: Only text tokens use the embedding grid; the image goes through the separate image encoder on the right.

misconceptions.claim: An image is represented by four tokens, as drawn.
misconceptions.correction: The drawing is schematic; Gemma uses 256 soft tokens per image (p.522).

misconceptions.claim: The decoder blocks are different for image and text positions.
misconceptions.correction: There is one stack of decoder blocks that processes the merged sequence.

takeaways: Figure 16.6: text goes through the embedding matrix to become hard tokens, the image goes through the image encoder to become soft tokens, and both are merged into one sequence for the decoder blocks.
Soft tokens fill the positions of the `` placeholders in the text.
The drawing uses 4 image tokens for clarity; Gemma actually uses 256.

questions.question: In figure 16.6, what produces the orange 'soft' tokens?
questions.explanation: The orange squares come out of the trapezoid labelled 'Image encoder'. The embedding matrix and tokenizer produce hard tokens, and the decoder blocks only consume the merged sequence.

questions.question: Where in the merged sequence do the soft tokens go?
questions.answer: In the positions of the `` placeholder tokens, between the hard tokens for 'What is' and '?'.
questions.explanation: The bottom row of figure 16.6 shows green, green, four orange, green, matching the order of the text tokens.

questions.question: Why does the figure show only one Transformer stack rather than separate stacks for text and image?
questions.answer: Because after splicing, all positions are vectors of the same hidden size, so a single decoder stack processes them uniformly; the multimodality is handled entirely on the input side.
questions.explanation: This is the point of p.522: the Transformer is a general sequence model.

questions.question: What are the shape and dtype of `image` after `np.array(keras.utils.load_img(image_path))`?
questions.explanation: load_img returns an RGB PIL image by default; np.array converts it to an HWC uint8 array.

questions.question: How many soft tokens represent one image in the real Gemma model, compared with the figure?
options: 256 in Gemma, 4 drawn in the figure
questions.answer: 256 in Gemma, 4 drawn in the figure
questions.explanation: p.522 gives 256 patches per image; 2560 is the vector dimension, not the count.

questions.question: Without looking, can you label the five parts of figure 16.6 (text embedding, image encoder, hard tokens, soft tokens, Transformer) and say which carry trainable weights?
questions.answer: Text embedding matrix, image encoder, and the Transformer decoder blocks have weights; hard and soft tokens are activations.
questions.explanation: Distinguishing parameters from activations is key to understanding what training updates.
